speaker: Sholto Douglas
title: Is RL + LLMs enough for AGI? — Sholto Douglas & Trenton Bricken
question: In reinforcement learning for large language models, why do training curves jump sharply right away instead of showing the long flat plateau seen in classic game-playing RL?
guest: You do need to be able to get reward sometimes in order to learn. In the Alpha variants, one player always wins, so you always get a reward signal one way or the other. But in the kinds of tasks we're talking about, you need to actually succeed at your task sometimes. Language models luckily have this wonderful prior over the tasks that we care about. If you look at all the old papers from 2017, the learning curves always look flat as they're figuring out the basic mechanics of the world, and then there's this spike up as they learn to exploit easy rewards—almost like a sigmoid—and then it continues on as it learns to maximize the game. I think the LLM curves look a bit different in that there isn't that dead zone at the beginning, because they already know how to solve some of the basic tasks. So you get this initial spike, and that's what people are talking about when they say you can learn from one example. That one example is just teaching you to pull out backtracking and format your answer correctly, which lets you get some reward initially conditional on your pretraining knowledge, and then the rest is learning more complex stuff.

points.core: Reinforcement learning requires occasional task successes to generate any usable reward gradient.
points.note: Accept: policies must hit non-zero reward on some rollouts to learn, unlike two-player self-play where one side always wins. Do not credit: generic claims that RL needs data or compute.

points.core: Pretrained language models skip the initial exploration plateau by already solving basic tasks.
points.note: Accept: strong pretraining priors eliminate the flat dead zone of from-scratch RL because the base policy already achieves non-zero pass rates. Do not credit: vague praise of scale or transformer architectures.

points.core: Sharp early gains from minimal examples mainly elicit formatting habits over preexisting knowledge.
points.note: Accept: one-shot or early RL spikes unlock latent pretraining capabilities by teaching answer formatting or backtracking rather than teaching new domain knowledge from scratch. Do not credit: claiming one-shot RL proves models learn complex domains with almost no compute.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The main reason is that the model doesn't start from scratch. In classic game-playing RL (Atari, Go from random initialization), the agent begins with a random policy that almost never stumbles onto reward, so it spends a long time exploring before any learning signal appears; that is the flat plateau. Only once it occasionally succeeds can gradients start reinforcing useful behavior.

A pretrained LLM, by contrast, already has broad knowledge, language competence, and reasonable problem-solving priors. On day one it succeeds on a meaningful fraction of tasks, so reward is dense enough to give useful gradients immediately. There is no exploration desert to cross.

The early jump is also often "cheap" learning: the model quickly picks up the task's surface requirements, such as the expected output format, how to use the tools, the appropriate response length, or quirks of the grader. These are small adjustments to existing capabilities rather than new skills, so they move the reward quickly. After that fast phase, curves typically flatten into slower gains as the model has to genuinely improve its reasoning or strategy.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Classic game-playing RL typically starts *tabula rasa* with randomly initialized weights. In sparse-reward games, an untrained agent must wander blindly through vast action spaces while learning basic representations from scratch, creating a long flat plateau until random exploration finally stumbles onto rewarding trajectories.

By contrast, RL for large language models begins from a heavily pretrained (and often instruction-tuned) policy. Because pretraining already imbues the model with language fluency, world knowledge, and latent reasoning strategies, the starting policy assigns non-zero probability to successful completions at step zero. Sampled rollouts therefore hit positive rewards immediately, bypassing the cold-start exploration bottleneck and providing informative policy gradients from the very first batch.

Furthermore, early RL updates do not need to invent new skills from nothing; they mainly sharpen the existing output distribution, rapidly shifting probability mass toward required answer formats and already-known high-reward behaviors before slower capability gains begin.

The main reason is that an LLM doesn't start RL from scratch. Classic game-playing agents like DQN on Atari begin with random weights. They have to stumble onto reward through near-random exploration, often for millions of frames, and learn perception and representations at the same time. With rewards that sparse, there's almost no gradient signal at first, so the curve stays flat until a lucky behavior gets reinforced.

A pretrained, often instruction-tuned, language model is very different. It already solves a meaningful fraction of prompts correctly, so even sparse correctness rewards come back nonzero from the first batch. Policy-gradient methods like PPO or GRPO can then immediately raise the probability of good completions the model can already produce. Much of the early jump is this reweighting, or "elicitation," of existing skills rather than learning new ones. Cheap fixes also contribute: following the required answer format, stopping cleanly, and matching the grader's expectations can lift reward quickly. Later gains, such as longer reasoning chains, tend to come more slowly. The pretraining prior has essentially already done the hard exploration, which is why there's no plateau.

In classic game-playing RL, agents usually start from random weights with no knowledge of the environment. They must rely on blind trial-and-error exploration just to stumble upon their first sparse rewards, producing a long flat plateau before meaningful learning begins.

In contrast, reinforcement learning for large language models starts from a richly pretrained—and often supervised fine-tuned—policy rather than from scratch. Because the model already understands language, concepts, and task structure, it places substantial probability mass on valid, high-reward responses from step zero. When multiple completions are sampled during the very first updates, some already succeed while others fail, immediately providing a clear advantage signal and strong gradients without a prolonged exploration phase. Early LLM RL therefore works primarily by sharpening and amplifying capabilities the base model already possesses—shifting probability mass toward preferred styles, formats, or reasoning paths—rather than discovering basic skills and environment dynamics from tabula rasa.

answers.answer: Classic game-playing RL typically starts from a randomly initialized policy, so in sparse-reward environments the agent must explore blindly for a long time before stumbling into rewarding trajectories and learning how the task works, producing a long flat plateau. Reinforcement learning for large language models instead starts from a heavily pretrained (and often supervised fine-tuned) model.
